Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 86, verses 1–3:

Makkiyya, and its verses are 17 [revealed after Surat al-Balad]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky and the night-comer.﴾ "Al-najm al-thaqib" means the bright, piercing one. It is as if it pierces the darkness with its light so that it penetrates it, as it has been said: "durri'" (a star), because it repels (yadra'uhu) it, that is, pushes it away. It is described as "al-tariq" because it appears at night, just as one who comes at night is called "tariq." Or it is because it strikes the jinn (yatruq al-jinna), that is, it hits them (yasukkuhu). The intended meaning is the genus of stars, or the genus of the shooting stars with which the devils are pelted.

If you say: "Wa ma adraka ma al-tariq (﴿And what will make you know what the night-comer is?﴾) resembles nothing but the translation of one word by another, "al-najm al-thaqib" (the piercing star). So explain to me what benefit lies beneath it?"

I say: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to swear by the piercing star, magnifying it for the wondrous power and subtle wisdom known in it, and to draw attention to this. So He brought in what is a common attribute between it and others, namely "al-tariq," then said: ﴿And what will make you know what the night-comer is?﴾ Then He explained it by saying: ﴿The piercing star.﴾ All of this is to display the greatness of its status, as He said: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars. And indeed, it is a great oath, if you only knew.﴾ (56:75–76)

It is narrated that Abu Talib was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when a star fell and the whole area was filled with light. Abu Talib was alarmed and said: "What is this?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "This is a star that was thrown, and it is one of the signs of Allah." Abu Talib was amazed, and then these verses were revealed. [[Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi mentioned this without an isnad.]]

Q. What is the response to the oath?

A. It is: "There is over every soul a guardian" (in'). Because "in" (inna) in the reading of one who reads "lamma" with shadda is not free of meaning, namely: "except that..." when it is a negation particle. And for one who reads it without shadda, with "ma" being a superfluous particle, it is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), and whichever of the two it is, it is among the things that the oath is introduced with. "A guardian" means one who watches over them, a supervisor, an observer, and this is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in ﴿And Allah is ever over all things an Observer﴾ and ﴿And Allah is ever over all things a Keeper of account﴾.

It has also been said: it is an angel who guards its deeds and records for it whatever good and evil it earns.

And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There are assigned to the believer one hundred and sixty angels who ward off from him, as flies are warded off from a bowl of honey. Were the servant left to himself for the blink of an eye, the devils would snatch him away." [Narrated by al-Tabarani from the narration of Ufayr ibn Ma'dan, from Sulaym ibn 'Amir, from Abu Umamah, with it being more complete than this. And Ufayr is weak.]

**Question:** What is the connection between His saying ﴿So let man look﴾ and what precedes it?

**Answer:** Its connection to what precedes it is that when He mentioned that over every soul there is a guardian, He followed it with an exhortation to the human being to reflect on the beginning of his affair and his first origin, so that he would know that the One who originated him is able to restore him and to recompense him. Then he would act for the Day of restoration and recompense, and would not have recorded against him by his guardian except what would gladden him in his final end.

**"From what was he created?"** This is an interrogative whose answer is: ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid.﴾ *Dafq* (gushing) means: pouring forth, propelled out. The meaning of *dafiq* (gushing) is that it is attributed to *al-dafq*, which is a verbal noun from *dafaqa*, like *laban* (milky) and *tamar* (dated). Or it is a metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*), while the gushing in reality belongs to its possessor.

He did not say "two waters," because they mix in the womb and become one when the creation of the human begins.

﴿From between the backbone and the ribs﴾: from between the backbone of the man and the ribs (*al-taraʾib*) of the woman. The *taraʾib* are the bones of the chest, where the necklace sits.

It has been read as *al-sulb* with two fathas and as *al-sulb* with two dammas. In it there are four dialectal forms: *sulb*, *sulb*, *sulb*, and *salib*. Al-ʿAjjaj said:

*"Plump of bones, ample of the thigh-ring,*
*in a waist like a well-tanned strap."*

*Al-rayya* is the feminine of *al-rayyan* (full, plump), meaning soft of bones, fleshy at the place of the *al-khadam*, which is the anklet. *Al-mukhaddam* with the doubled letter is in the form of the passive participle. *Al-sulb* with two dammas, with two fathas, or with a damma then a sukun, means the bones of the back, and what is intended here is the waist. The *fi* in "in a waist" means *maʿa* (with): she is described with these attributes, along with having a slender, soft waist, like a well-tanned strap, in the form of the passive participle, meaning twisted. It is said: *adama baynahuma* (with the hamza short or long), meaning he joined and reconciled them. Or it means one to which a tanned hide has been given. Or *layyin al-adama* (with two fathas), where *al-adama* is the tanned, prepared skin, from *adamahu* with the lengthened vowel, meaning he gave it a hide. *Al-fakhma* with a damma means largeness and the looseness of the two legs. *Al-fakhma* with a fatha is its adjectival form.

It has been said: the bone and the sinew are from the man, and the flesh and the blood are from the woman.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 86, verses 8–10:

The pronoun in "innahu" (that is, His) refers to the Creator, because the context ("khalaq," who created) indicates Him. The meaning is: Indeed, He who created man from a drop of fluid (nutfah) initially, is truly capable (qadir) of "ruj'ihi" (returning him), that is, of bringing him back again, with clear and absolute capability; nothing is difficult or incapacitating for Him [[The phrase "la yaltath 'alayhi" (nothing is hard for Him) — in the Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "iltatha fi 'amalihi" means he was slow in his work. (Ed.)]]. This is like the saying of the poet: "Indeed I am poor" [[The phrase "like His saying, indeed I am poor": that is, the poet, where he said: "Though he is guided by the cold of her fangs on high, / I am poorer than him, indeed I am poor." (Ed.) This witness was explained earlier in this volume, page 23, so refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]], "yawma tubla" (on the day when secrets are examined) is in the accusative, governed by "ruj'ihi" (its verb). Whoever takes the pronoun in "ruj'ihi" to refer to the water and interprets "return" as its return to its place of emission from the spine and the ribs, or to the urethra, or to its first state, makes the time-expression accusative by an implied verb.

"Al-sara'ir" (the secrets) are what is concealed in the hearts of beliefs, intentions and others, and what is hidden of deeds.

"Wa bala'uha" (and their examination): knowing them and scrutinizing them, and distinguishing between what was good in them and what was corrupt. It is reported from al-Hasan that he heard a man reciting:

"There will remain for her, in the hidden part of the heart and the inner breast, / a secret of love, on the day when secrets are tested." [[When I tried to forget her, a intercessor said: / "From love, the appointment of forgetting is the graves."

"There will remain for her, in the hidden part of the heart and the inner breast, / a secret of love, on the day when secrets are tested."

Belonging to Majnun of Banu 'Amir, the companion of Layla al-'Amiriyya. He forgot her and turned away from her, and the poet likened the love's sending of him and its bearing him to lasting affection to the saying of the speaker in the manner of explicit metaphor (tasrihiyya). Calling love an intercessor is a reinforcement (tarshih). "Min" is explanatory. It may be abstract (tajridiyya), indicating that love reached the limit of pleasure, so that it was carried to lasting affection, and another was extracted from it and the verb ascribed to it. It may also be partitive (tab'idiyya), indicating that part of it suffices for intercession. His saying "al-maqabir" means entering them, a metaphor for death. The intended meaning is permanence, as shown by what follows. "Mudmar al-qalb" means what is hidden in the heart, or "mudmar" is the heart itself. "Tubla" is in the active voice, meaning "tufna" (perish).

It may also be in the passive, meaning "tukhtabar" (be tested). "Al-hasha" with a fatha is conjoined to "al-qalb" and is more general than it, indicating that love is also in other than the heart.]]

Then he said: "How heedless is he of what is in 'wa al-sama'i wa al-tariq'?" [[Surah al-Tariq 86:1–2 be read as a witness.]] "Fa-ma lahu" (So he has no) "min quwwah" (power) — no defense within himself by which he can resist, "wa la nasir" (nor any helper), nor any protector who can prevent Him from him.

He named the rain *raj'an* (return) just as he named it *awban* (returning). He said:

*"Lofty and towering, the summit of the mountain's peak, which none shelters but the clouds, the rain-bearing winds and the torrents."*

[[This verse is by al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhali, lamenting his son. It is also said to describe a man as *ribaʾ*, meaning a lookout, from *rabaʾa* and *irtabaʾa*, meaning to rise up to look at a matter. From this comes *al-rabiʾa* (the sentry). Its genitive construction with *shammaʾ* (idafa, the attributive genitive, where the noun governs an adjective in the sense of its object) is of the type where the adjective is attributed to its object. *Shammaʾ* is a fortress raised high, from *shamm*, meaning height.

*Qulla* (the peak) of a mountain and its *qunna* are its head and highest point. *Awb* means bees, because they go out and return (*yaʾūbu*) to their hive. It may also mean rain, because according to the Arabs' belief its origin is from the seas of the earth, and then it returns (*yaʾūbu*) to them. *Sabal*, with a vowelled *ba*, means rain, from *asbaltu al-sitr*, when I let down and lowered the curtain. On the view that *awb* means bees, there is no contextual connection between them; on the view that it means rain, *sabal* is a synonym for it.]]

*Raj'* and *awb* are verbal nouns (taʾwīl). The Arabs believed that the cloud carries water from the seas of the earth and then sends it back to the earth. Or they intended an omen, so they named it *raj'* (return), and *awb*, so that it returns and comes back. It is also said that this is because God returns it from time to time. Al-Khansa said: *"Like the returning (rain) in the cloudy, flowing (sky)."*

*Al-ṣadʿ* (the cleft) is that from which the earth splits open with vegetation.

*"Lofty and towering, the summit of the mountain's peak, which none shelters but the clouds, the rain-bearing winds and the torrents."*

[[This verse is by al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhali, lamenting his son. It is also said to describe a man as *ribaʾ*, meaning a lookout, from *rabaʾa* and *irtabaʾa*, meaning to rise up to look at a matter. From this comes *al-rabiʾa* (the sentry). Its genitive construction with *shammaʾ* (idafa, the attributive genitive, where the noun governs an adjective in the sense of its object) is of the type where the adjective is attributed to its object. *Shammaʾ* is a fortress raised high, from *shamm*, meaning height.

*Qulla* (the peak) of a mountain and its *qunna* are its head and highest point. *Awb* means bees, because they go out and return (*yaʾūbu*) to their hive. It may also mean rain, because according to the Arabs' belief its origin is from the seas of the earth, and then it returns (*yaʾūbu*) to them. *Sabal*, with a vowelled *ba*, means rain, from *asbaltu al-sitr*, when I let down and lowered the curtain. On the view that *awb* means bees, there is no contextual connection between them; on the view that it means rain, *sabal* is a synonym for it.]]

إِنَّهُمْ (they, i.e. the people of Makkah) يعملون المكايد في إبطال أمر الله وإطفاء نور الحق — "they devise schemes to nullify the command of God and to extinguish the light of the truth", وأنا أقابلهم بكيدى: من استدراجى لهم وانتظاري بهم الميقات الذي وقته للانتصار منهم — "and I counter them with My scheme: by drawing them on gradually (istidraj) and by My waiting for them until the appointed time which I have set for taking vengeance upon them".

فَمَهِّلِ الْكافِرِينَ — "so give respite to the disbelievers", يعنى لا تدع بهلاكهم ولا تستعجل به — "meaning: do not pray for their destruction, and do not hasten it", أَمْهِلْهُمْ رُوَيْداً — "give them respite, a little while", أى إمهالا يسيرا — "that is, a brief respite". وكرّر وخالف بين اللفظين لزيادة التسكين منه والتصبير — "He repeated [the idea] and varied the two expressions to increase the consolation and the encouragement to patience."

عن رسول الله ﷺ «من قرأ سورة الطارق أعطاه الله بعدد كل نجم في السماء عشر حسنات» — "From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): «Whoever recites Surah al-Tariq, God will grant him ten good deeds for every star in the heaven.»" [[أخرجه الواحدي والثعلبي وابن مردويه بالسند إلى أبى بن كعب.]] — "Related by al-Wahidi, al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b."
